claim: Adult stem cells maintain self-renewing tissues.
source: How adult stem cells maintain self-renewing tissues is commonly assessed by analysing clonal data from in vivo cell lineage-tracing assays.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and introduction.

claim: Models of cell fate choice in homeostatic tissues can be categorized by exactly two 'universality classes'.
source: Here, we show that models of cell fate choice can, in homeostatic tissues, be categorized by exactly two 'universality classes', whereby models of the same class predict, under asymptotic conditions, the same clonal statistics.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by mathematical analysis and numerical simulations presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Models of the same universality class predict the same clonal statistics under asymptotic conditions.
source: Here, we show that models of cell fate choice can, in homeostatic tissues, be categorized by exactly two 'universality classes', whereby models of the same class predict, under asymptotic conditions, the same clonal statistics.
evidence: This is demonstrated through mathematical analysis and numerical simulations shown in Figures 2-4.

claim: The two universality classes relate to generalizations of the canonical asymmetric vs. symmetric stem cell self-renewal strategies.
source: Those classes relate to generalizations of the canonical asymmetric vs. symmetric stem cell self-renewal strategies and are distinguished by a conservation law.
evidence: This is explained through the definition of GIA and GPA models and their relationship to classical IA and PA strategies.

claim: The two universality classes are distinguished by a conservation law.
source: Those classes relate to generalizations of the canonical asymmetric vs. symmetric stem cell self-renewal strategies and are distinguished by a conservation law.
evidence: The manuscript explains that GIA models conserve the number of R-cells while GPA models do not.

claim: Self-renewal models of the same universality class cannot be distinguished by clonal data only under asymptotic conditions.
source: This poses both challenges and opportunities to identify stem cell self-renewal strategies: while under asymptotic conditions, self-renewal models of the same universality class cannot be distinguished by clonal data only, models of different classes can be distinguished by simple means.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the convergence of clone size distributions shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Models of different universality classes can be distinguished by simple means.
source: This poses both challenges and opportunities to identify stem cell self-renewal strategies: while under asymptotic conditions, self-renewal models of the same universality class cannot be distinguished by clonal data only, models of different classes can be distinguished by simple means.
evidence: This is supported by the different asymptotic distributions (Exponential vs. Normal) predicted by GPA and GIA models.

claim: Adult stem cells persistently produce tissue cells through cell division and differentiation.
source: Adult stem cells are the key players for maintaining and renewing biological tissue, due to their ability to persistently produce tissue cells through cell division and differentiation (National Institute of Health, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the National Institute of Health.

claim: Imbalanced proliferation may lead to hyperplasia and cancer.
source: For maintaining tissues in a homeostatic state, it is crucial that stem cells adopt suitable self-renewal strategies, a pattern of stem cell fate choices that balances proliferation and differentiation; otherwise, imbalanced proliferation may lead to hyperplasia and cancer.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about tissue homeostasis.

claim: Two classical stem cell self-renewal strategies have been proposed: Invariant Asymmetric division (IA) and Population Asymmetry (PA).
source: Classically, two stem cell self-renewal strategies have been proposed (Potten and Loeffler, 1990; Simons and Clevers, 2011a): following the Invariant Asymmetric division (IA) strategy, stem cells undertake only asymmetric divisions, whose outcome is one differentiating cell and one stem cell as daughter cells. The other proposed strategy, Population Asymmetry (PA) (Potten and Loeffler, 1990; Simons and Clevers, 2011a; Watt and Hogan, 2000; Klein and Simons, 2011), features additionally symmetric divisions, which produce either two stem cells or two differentiating cells as daughters, yet in balanced proportions.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: In the IA strategy, stem cells undertake only asymmetric divisions producing one differentiating cell and one stem cell.
source: following the Invariant Asymmetric division (IA) strategy, stem cells undertake only asymmetric divisions, whose outcome is one differentiating cell and one stem cell as daughter cells.
evidence: This is a definition cited from prior literature.

claim: The PA strategy features symmetric divisions that produce either two stem cells or two differentiating cells in balanced proportions.
source: The other proposed strategy, Population Asymmetry (PA) (Potten and Loeffler, 1990; Simons and Clevers, 2011a; Watt and Hogan, 2000; Klein and Simons, 2011), features additionally symmetric divisions, which produce either two stem cells or two differentiating cells as daughters, yet in balanced proportions.
evidence: This is a definition cited from prior literature.

claim: Both IA and PA patterns of cell fate choice leave the number of cells on average unchanged and can maintain homeostasis.
source: Both patterns of cell fate choice leave the number of cells on average unchanged and thus can maintain homeostasis.
evidence: This is explained as a logical consequence of the definitions of IA and PA strategies.

claim: Direct observation of cell divisions is rarely possible in vivo.
source: Assessing stem cell self-renewal strategies experimentally is difficult in vivo, since direct observation of cell divisions is rarely possible.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation of experimental methods.

claim: Genetic cell lineage-tracing assays allow obtaining statistics of clones.
source: Yet, through genetic cell lineage-tracing assays, the statistics of clones – the progeny of individual cells – can be obtained, and via mathematical modeling assessing cell fate dynamics became possible.
evidence: This is stated as an established experimental approach.

claim: Several studies suggested that population asymmetry prevails in many mouse tissues.
source: With such an approach several studies suggested that population asymmetry prevails in many mouse tissues (e.g. Clayton et al., 2007; Lopez-Garcia et al., 2010; Simons and Clevers, 2011b; Doupé et al., 2012; Klein et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: The Dynamic Heterogeneity (DH) model features some degree of cell fate plasticity.
source: However, the interpretation of those studies has been challenged by a suggested alternative self-renewal strategy, called Dynamic Heterogeneity (DH), featuring some degree of cell fate plasticity (Greulich and Simons, 2016).
evidence: This is cited from prior work by Greulich and Simons.

claim: In the DH model, all stem cell divisions are asymmetric.
source: In this model, all stem cell divisions are asymmetric, yet it is in agreement with the experimental clonal data that had previously been shown to agree also with the population asymmetry strategy.
evidence: This is a description of the DH model from prior work.

claim: The DH model is in agreement with experimental clonal data that also agrees with the PA strategy.
source: In this model, all stem cell divisions are asymmetric, yet it is in agreement with the experimental clonal data that had previously been shown to agree also with the population asymmetry strategy.
evidence: This is cited from prior work by Greulich and Simons.

claim: There exist two particular classes of stem cell self-renewal strategies: one generating an Exponential distribution of clone sizes and one generating a Normal distribution.
source: In particular, we find that there exist two particular classes of stem cell self-renewal strategies: one class of models which all generate an Exponential distribution of clone sizes (the number of cells in a clone) after sufficiently large time, and one which generates a Normal distribution under sufficiently fast stem cell proliferation.
evidence: This is demonstrated through mathematical analysis and numerical simulations in the Results section.

claim: The two classes are differentiated by whether or not a subset of cells is conserved.
source: Crucially, these two classes are not differentiated via the classical definitions of symmetric and asymmetric stem cell divisions, but by whether or not a subset of cells is conserved.
evidence: This is explained through the definition of GIA and GPA models and their conservation properties.

claim: These classes bear resemblance to 'universality classes' known from statistical physics.
source: These classes thus bear resemblance to 'universality classes' known from statistical physics, as suggested in Klein and Simons, 2011.
evidence: This is an analogy drawn to concepts from statistical physics, with citation to prior work.

claim: The conditions for the emergence of universality are not always fulfilled in real tissues.
source: Notably, however, we find that the conditions for the emergence of universality are not always fulfilled in real tissues, which provides chances, but also further challenges, for the identification of stem cell fate choices in homeostatic tissues.
evidence: This is discussed as an implication of the theoretical findings.

claim: The IA model corresponds to r=0 (only asymmetric divisions occur).
source: the IA model is defined by r=0, that is, only asymmetric divisions occur.
evidence: This is a mathematical definition of the IA model.

claim: For the IA model, the number of stem cells is strictly conserved.
source: However, only for the IA model is the number of stem cells strictly conserved, that is, no gain or loss of stem cells is possible.
evidence: This follows from the mathematical definition of the IA model where r=0.

claim: Exponential clone size distributions prevail for most mouse tissues.
source: By a series of lineage-tracing experiments it was confirmed that Exponential clone size distributions prevail for most mouse tissues, which thus exclude the IA model and support the PA strategy (Clayton et al., 2007; Lopez-Garcia et al., 2010; Simons and Clevers, 2011b; Doupé et al., 2012; Klein et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: The DH model predicts clonal statistics that are indistinguishable from the PA model.
source: Notably, the DH model only features asymmetric divisions (in that daughter cells are of different type), like the IA model, yet the DH model predicts clonal statistics that are indistinguishable from the PA model (Greulich and Simons, 2016).
evidence: This is cited from prior work by Greulich and Simons.

claim: The PA and DH model cannot be distinguished via plain clonal data.
source: This means that in view of the existing clonal data for mouse tissues, the DH model, may as well describe the real cell fate dynamics. More fundamentally, this implies that the PA and DH model cannot be distinguished via plain clonal data, which poses fundamental limitations to the common approach to use lineage tracing for determining cell fate choices.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both models predict the same clonal statistics.

claim: The classical definition of asymmetric and symmetric divisions is not always suitable to distinguish cell fate strategies in view of clonal data alone.
source: This demonstrates that the classical definition of asymmetric and symmetric divisions is not always suitable to distinguish cell fate strategies in view of clonal data alone.
evidence: This is inferred from the inability to distinguish PA and DH models despite their different division types.

claim: For homeostatic networks, an SCC with dominant eigenvalue μ=0 is at the apex, while other SCCs have μ<0.
source: For homeostatic networks, an SCC with dominant eigenvalue μ=0 is at the apex, while other SCCs have μ<0.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1 and explained in the text and Appendix.

claim: The Renewing compartment (R) consists of the apex SCC with μ=0.
source: We distinguish two compartments, the Renewing compartment ℛ, consisting of the apex SCC, with μ=0, and the Committed compartment 𝒞 consisting of the remainder, with μ<0.
evidence: This is defined in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The Committed compartment (C) consists of all SCCs with μ<0.
source: We distinguish two compartments, the Renewing compartment ℛ, consisting of the apex SCC, with μ=0, and the Committed compartment 𝒞 consisting of the remainder, with μ<0.
evidence: This is defined in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Cells in states forming R have the potential to return to any state within the same compartment and this population maintains itself.
source: Importantly, cells in states forming ℛ have the potential to return to any state within the same compartment and this population maintains itself.
evidence: This follows from the definition of strongly connected components and the eigenvalue condition.

claim: The progeny of each cell in the committed compartment will eventually be lost.
source: Instead, the cell population in 𝒞 would vanish without external input, since the combined dominant eigenvalue of all those SCCs is negative (it is the maximum of all SCCs' μk<0), thus the progeny of each cell in the committed compartment will eventually be lost.
evidence: This follows from the negative eigenvalue condition for the committed compartment.

claim: GIA models are those which only exhibit R→R+C divisions in the renewing compartment.
source: Generalized Invariant Asymmetry (GIA) models are those which only exhibit R→R+C divisions in the renewing compartment, while Generalized Population Asymmetry (GPA) are models for which such restriction does not hold.
evidence: This is a definition introduced in the manuscript.

claim: GPA models are those for which the restriction to only R→R+C divisions does not hold.
source: Generalized Invariant Asymmetry (GIA) models are those which only exhibit R→R+C divisions in the renewing compartment, while Generalized Population Asymmetry (GPA) are models for which such restriction does not hold.
evidence: This is a definition introduced in the manuscript.

claim: For GIA models, the number of cells in R is strictly conserved.
source: We note that the two classes are equivalently characterized by a conservation law: For GIA models, the number of cells in ℛ is strictly conserved, while for GPA models, no such conservation law holds.
evidence: This follows from the definition of GIA models where only R→R+C divisions occur.

claim: For GPA models, no conservation law holds.
source: We note that the two classes are equivalently characterized by a conservation law: For GIA models, the number of cells in ℛ is strictly conserved, while for GPA models, no such conservation law holds.
evidence: This follows from the definition of GPA models which allow R→R+R and R→C+C divisions.

claim: The IA model is a GIA model.
source: Naturally, the previously discussed IA model is a GIA model and the PA model is a GPA model.
evidence: This follows from the definitions of IA and GIA models.

claim: The PA model is a GPA model.
source: Naturally, the previously discussed IA model is a GIA model and the PA model is a GPA model.
evidence: This follows from the definitions of PA and GPA models.

claim: The DH model is of the GPA category.
source: Notably, the DH model (Equation 2) is of the GPA category, since in that model S and D cells form a single SCC at the apex of the lineage hierarchy, and thus they are both part of ℛ.
evidence: This is explained through analysis of the DH model structure.

claim: A division S→S+D in the DH model corresponds to R→R+R in terms of compartments.
source: Therefore, a division S→S+D in the DH model, which is asymmetric in the conventional sense, corresponds to R→R+R in terms of compartments (Equation 9) and thus it is a generalised symmetric division.
evidence: This is explained through the compartment analysis of the DH model.

claim: PA and DH models both predict the same type of clone size distribution, an Exponential one.
source: According to this classification, PA and DH models are both in the same category (GPA), and indeed, both predict the same type of clone size distribution, an Exponential one (Greulich and Simons, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and the theoretical analysis in this manuscript.

claim: For every simulated GIA model, the mean clone size saturates at a plateau value.
source: While for every simulated GIA model, n¯s saturates at a plateau value, it steadily increases for every GPA model.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2(a) from numerical simulations.

claim: For every simulated GPA model, the mean clone size steadily increases.
source: While for every simulated GIA model, n¯s saturates at a plateau value, it steadily increases for every GPA model.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2(b) from numerical simulations.

claim: In non-conserved multi-type branching processes, the clone number decreases through progressive extinction of clones.
source: However, in non-conserved multi-type branching processes, as GPA models are, the clone number Nc decreases through progressive extinction of clones (Haccou et al., 2005), and therefore n¯s increases, despite the cell population as a whole staying stationary.
evidence: This is cited from branching process theory.

claim: All simulated GPA models predict asymptotically the same rescaled clone size distribution, namely a standard Exponential distribution.
source: As conjectured, all simulated GPA models shown in panel (b) predict asymptotically the same rescaled clone size distribution, namely a standard Exponential distribution.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3(b) from numerical simulations.

claim: Different models within the GPA class cannot be distinguished in the long-term limit, since they differ only by the mean clone size.
source: This means that different models within the GPA class cannot be distinguished in the long-term limit, since they differ only by the mean clone size, which is a free fit parameter.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that all GPA models converge to the same rescaled distribution.

claim: All GPA models are expected to generate Exponential clone size distributions for large times.
source: In the Appendix, 'Asymptotic clone size distributions: mathematical analysis', we reason that all GPA models are expected to generate Exponential clone size distributions for large times t.
evidence: This is derived in the Appendix through mathematical analysis.

claim: The GIA and GPA model classes each represent a universality class.
source: Hence, the GIA and GPA model classes, each represent a universality class, that is, a scaling limit exists in which all models of the same class yield the same rescaled clonal statistics.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the mathematical and numerical analysis.

claim: Intrinsic limitations exist for identifying strategies of stem cell self-renewal through clonal data from cell lineage-tracing experiments.
source: Our analysis shows that intrinsic limitations exist for identifying strategies of stem cell self-renewal through clonal data from cell lineage-tracing experiments.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the Discussion section based on the results.

claim: Different models of cell fate choice can generate the same type of clonal statistics.
source: This is due to different models of cell fate choice generating the same type of clonal statistics (clone size distributions), so that model inference based on clonal statistics – currently still the most prevalent method to determine stem cell self-renewal strategies – fails to distinguish them.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the numerical and mathematical analysis in the Results section.

claim: The feature that different models asymptotically generate the same statistics corresponds to universality, as known from statistical physics.
source: The feature that different models asymptotically generate the same statistics is a form of weak convergence of random variables (Billingsley, 1968) and corresponds to universality, as known from statistical physics.
evidence: This is an analogy drawn to concepts from statistical physics and probability theory.

claim: Models of cell fate choice cannot in general be distinguished with further resolution beyond the R vs. C categorization of cell types.
source: Hence, our analysis shows that models of cell fate choice cannot in general be distinguished with further resolution beyond the R vs. C categorization of cell types.
evidence: This is concluded from the universality of clonal statistics within each model class.

claim: The universality of the model dynamics shows that effective, simplistic models are often equally accurate to model experimental data.
source: The universality of the model dynamics also shows that effective, simplistic models are often equally accurate to model experimental data, yet with a higher statistical power due to less free parameters.
evidence: This is a practical implication of the universality finding.

claim: Room remains for model distinction in regimes where the limiting conditions for asymptotic distributions are not fulfilled.
source: While at first glance, this analysis seems to discourage efforts to unravel details of cell fate dynamics, room remains in regimes where the limiting conditions for asymptotic distributions are not fulfilled.
evidence: This is discussed as an opportunity for future research.

claim: If fast cycling committed progenitor cells are present while stem cells are slow cycling, details of the model dynamics may affect the shape of the clone size distribution.
source: In particular, if fast cycling committed progenitor cells are present, while stem cells are slow cycling, then the condition that the division rate of R-cells is much larger than the cell loss rate is not fulfilled. In that case, details of the model dynamics may affect the shape of the clone size distribution and thus allow distinction between models.
evidence: This is discussed as a scenario where universality breaks down.

claim: When an Exponential clone size distribution is observed, it could indicate either a GIA model with high activity of committed progenitor cells, or a GPA model.
source: However, caution should be given when an Exponential clone size distribution is observed, since this could indicate either a GIA model with high activity of committed progenitor cells, or a GPA model.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that GIA models can also produce Exponential distributions under certain conditions.

claim: Markovian approximations are increasingly accurate at long times because of the feature of universality.
source: At long times, however, Markovian approximations are increasingly accurate, precisely because of the feature of universality.
evidence: This is explained as a consequence of universality.

claim: Many limitations exist to determining cell fate trajectories via scRNA-seq data analysis.
source: However, many limitations to this method exist, discussed in Weinreb et al., 2018, and neither reversible trajectories nor the modes of cell division, such as asymmetric vs symmetric divisions, can be inferred.
evidence: This is cited from prior literature discussing limitations of scRNA-seq.

claim: Intravital live imaging allows tracing individual clones over time.
source: Intravital live imaging, on the other hand, allows to trace individual clones over time (Ritsma et al., 2012; Pittet and Weissleder, 2011; Hara et al., 2014; Rompolas et al., 2016), and thus can obtain details of cell fate trajectories, yet this technique is limited to few tissue types which are accessible for invasive long-term imaging.
evidence: This is cited from prior literature on imaging techniques.

claim: Advanced model inference schemes that integrate data from different experimental sources might reveal details of stem cell self-renewal strategies.
source: Nonetheless, while each of those experimental assays alone is prone to limitations in defining self-renewal strategies, advanced model inference schemes, that integrate data from different experimental sources, might be the way forward in the future to finally reveal the details of stem cell self-renewal strategies.
evidence: This is proposed as a future direction for research.

claim: The clonal statistics of spatial models that include cell-extrinsic regulation of cell fate are, in the long term, the same as for the corresponding branching process models, except for one-dimensional arrangements of cells.
source: However, the clonal statistics of spatial models that include cell-extrinsic regulation of cell fate (models of the voter type [Clifford and Sudbury, 1973]) are, in the long term, the same as for the corresponding branching process models (Haccou et al., 2005), as Equations 3-5 are, except for one-dimensional arrangements of cells (as shown in Klein and Simons, 2011; Bramson and Griffeath, 1980).
evidence: This is cited from prior theoretical work on spatial models.

claim: The results cover cell dynamics in most renewing tissues, such as epithelial sheets or volumnar organs, but not (quasi-)one-dimensional arrangements of stem cells.
source: Thus, our results cover cell dynamics in most renewing tissues, such as epithelial sheets or volumnar organs, but not (quasi-)one-dimensional arrangements of stem cells, as found in the seminiferous tubule, or in intestinal crypts, where clonal statistics may differ.
evidence: This is inferred from the theoretical considerations about spatial arrangements.
